topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Transport APIs move bytes or datagrams, but the application must define a message contract. A TCP read is not one message, and a UDP send is not proof of delivery. This chapter sends a binary-safe framed TCP request through a loopback server and performs a separate local UDP exchange. It keeps framing, timeout, cleanup, and thread-failure handling visible instead of hiding them behind an unbounded demonstration loop.

topics.title: 15.1.1 Implementing TCP Servers
topics.summary: A TCP server accepts a connected socket and interprets an ordered stream of bytes. The application must delimit messages, for example with a fixed header containing a bounded body length. Validate that length before allocating the body. A clean EOF before a new header differs from an EOF partway through a header or body.

blocks.text: Define framing before implementing the parser. The book’s elementary protocol uses a four-byte unsigned length in network byte order followed by exactly that many payload bytes. The accepted maximum is 4096 bytes. The receiver validates the declared length before allocating the payload, so an oversized header does not request an arbitrary amount of memory. A length limit is a resource policy, not proof that the payload is semantically valid.

blocks.text: The header itself can arrive in fragments. Accumulate exactly four bytes, decode the value, validate the limit, and then accumulate the body. Clean EOF before a new header can mean no request; EOF after a partial header or before the declared body completes is truncation. A zero-length body is a complete empty frame, not a transport EOF. These distinctions are exercised more extensively in the supplemental codec tests.

topics.title: 15.1.2 Implementing TCP Clients
topics.summary: A client chooses an endpoint, connects, sends its request framing and body, and reads the response under the same protocol. Both send and receive may make partial progress. A send success reports acceptance by the local interface, not that the peer has processed the request. Application acknowledgments or response semantics establish that later fact.

blocks.text: Retry policy must consider whether an operation may already have been applied. Reconnecting and blindly resending a non-idempotent request can duplicate work. This example’s transformation is a pure byte reversal, so repeated requests have no external side effects, but a production update protocol would need request identity and duplicate-handling rules.

blocks.text: A client resolves or constructs the destination, creates a compatible socket, connects, sends a framed request, and reads the framed response. Each stage has a different failure meaning. A connection failure says the stream was not established through that attempt; a response timeout after sending leaves uncertainty about whether the server already processed the request. Retrying both cases identically can duplicate external effects.

blocks.text: Writes need a partial-progress loop. After a successful send of a prefix, advance the pointer and reduce the remaining count. On Linux, the helper uses MSG_NOSIGNAL for socket sends so a broken peer can be reported as an error without delivering SIGPIPE for that call. That option does not make the transfer transactional, and it does not apply to every non-socket write interface. (SOCKETSEND)

blocks.text: Reads require the same progress discipline. A response header can be split, the body can be empty, and the peer can close at any point. The response parser must enforce its own size bound rather than trusting a server merely because the connection was outbound. A compromised or defective peer is still a source of arbitrary bytes.

The response parser must enforce its own size bound rather than trusting a server merely because the connection was outbound. A compromised or defective peer is still a source of arbitrary bytes.

blocks.text: A total deadline should cover the intended operation, not be recreated every time progress occurs. The elementary socket helper applies bounded waits and per-call socket timeouts, which are useful safety measures for controlled fixtures but do not prove an absolute end-to-end request deadline. A slow peer can keep making small progress. The extended HarborRelay implementation carries a single steady-clock deadline through each framed operation.

blocks.text: A successful response should be validated at the application layer. The worked reverse service compares the exact returned byte string, including an embedded zero byte. It does not use C-string termination to decide payload length. For a request that changes durable state, a response would also need a documented acknowledgement meaning. “The bytes arrived” and “the transaction committed once” are different claims.

blocks.text: Datagrams can be lost, duplicated, or reordered, and a successful local send does not remove those possibilities. A loopback exchange is useful for testing API use but does not reproduce a lossy production network.

blocks.text: UDP sends discrete datagrams. Each receive obtains at most one datagram’s content rather than continuing a byte stream across unrelated messages. This preserves message boundaries but introduces a separate buffer-sizing obligation: an incoming datagram can be larger than the supplied receive buffer. The application must detect truncation and reject incomplete data rather than parsing a silently shortened message. (SOCKETRECV)

A packet that does not fit is not a valid shorter packet.

topics.title: 15.2.2 Handling Loss and Ordering at the Application Layer
topics.summary: An application can attach sequence numbers, acknowledgments, deadlines, and duplicate-detection state when its UDP use requires stronger semantics. Those mechanisms create another protocol with their own wraparound, replay, and resource limits. A sequence number alone neither authenticates the sender nor guarantees eventual delivery.

blocks.text: UDP applications must decide what loss, duplication, and reordering mean. A telemetry display may accept occasional loss and keep the newest sample. A command protocol may require acknowledgement, bounded retries, duplicate detection, and a way to determine whether a previous command took effect. topics.title: Failure clinic — A timeout that restarts forever
topics.summary: A service configures a five-second receive timeout and accepts a peer that sends one byte every four seconds. Every individual receive makes progress, yet the full request never finishes within five seconds. The implementation enforced a per-call inactivity policy, not the advertised total request deadline. Carry an absolute deadline through the entire header-and-body operation and recompute remaining time before each wait.
